title: Safety Leadership
osha_standards: OSH Act Section 5(a)(1) General Duty Clause
summary: Safety programs work when owners, managers, and supervisors treat worker safety as a core value and lead by example. OSHA recommends a written policy, clear roles, open communication, and rewarding workers who speak up.
talking_points: Leaders make worker safety and health a core value, as important as productivity, profit, and quality.
Supervisors set the example by following the same safety procedures they expect from workers.
Hold weekly or daily toolbox talks and review open safety items on a to-do list.
A written safety policy signed by top management should be shared with all workers, subcontractors, and temporary workers.
Give workers time and resources to take part in the safety program, and pledge that safety gets the budget it needs, such as safety equipment in the project budget.
Name a frontline person to lead safety efforts. Define responsibilities and hold people accountable.
Reward workers who report close calls, attend training, or do inspections. Successful programs reward workers who find problems rather than discipline them.
Workers should be able to report hazards without fear of retaliation, and to request a temporary stop to any work they believe is unsafe. Retaliation is illegal under Section 11(c).
site_hazards_to_check: No written safety policy shared with subs and temp workers
No named person leading safety on the job
Safety equipment missing from the project budget
No simple way for workers to report hazards, injuries, or close calls
Open safety items with no owner or follow-up
Supervisors not following the rules they set for the crew
discussion_questions: What does our leadership do on this job to show safety comes first?
How can any of us stop unsafe work, and who do we tell?
What happened the last time someone reported a hazard here?

attribution.notice: Adapted from OSHA published material. Reproduced with attribution for jobsite safety training; not an endorsement by OSHA.

flags: Verified against OSHA 3886 (Recommended Practices for Safety and Health Programs in Construction): core value, lead by example, toolbox talks and open-items to-do list, signed written policy shared with subs/temps, safety equipment in project budget, time for participation, frontline person, reward not discipline, empower workers to request temporary suspension of unsafe work, Section 11(c) anti-retaliation. All present.

Citations: OSH Act Section 11(c) is stated in the source and is correct for anti-retaliation. Section 5(a)(1) General Duty Clause is not stated in this source but is a valid statute; neither is a 1926 section, acceptable for a management-practice talk.

Non-blocking: OSHA 3886 is voluntary recommended practice, not a regulatory requirement; the talk phrases items as leadership practices, not legal mandates. Point 8 correctly limits 'illegal' to 11(c) retaliation.
